questions.q: State the null and alternative hypotheses for testing whether a new fertilizer increases the mean crop yield $\mu$, given a historical mean $\mu_0=50$ kg. Classify the test as one-tailed or two-tailed.
questions.answer: $H_0:\mu=50$. $H_a:\mu>50$. This is a one-tailed (right-tailed) test, since the alternative specifies a direction.

questions.q: Explain the difference between a one-tailed and a two-tailed hypothesis test, giving an example scenario for each.
questions.answer: A one-tailed test is used when the alternative hypothesis specifies a direction (e.g. testing whether a new drug \emph{increases} recovery rate). A two-tailed test is used when the alternative simply states the parameter differs from the claimed value, without specifying direction (e.g. testing whether a machine's mean output has changed at all, up or down).

questions.q: A test has $H_0:\mu=75$ vs $H_a:\mu\neq75$, and the sample data leads to rejecting $H_0$ at the 5% significance level. State, without further calculation, whether this data would also lead to rejection at the 1% level, justifying your answer.
questions.answer: Not necessarily — a stricter significance level (1%) requires stronger evidence (a smaller $p$-value) to reject $H_0$. If the $p$-value is very small (well below $0.01$), rejection would still occur at 1%; but if the $p$-value lies between $0.01$ and $0.05$, $H_0$ would be rejected at 5% but not at 1%.

sections.heading: Hypothesis test for a population mean (known σ)

questions.q: A machine fills bags with a claimed mean of $500$g, with known population standard deviation $\sigma=15$g. A sample of $n=36$ bags has mean $\bar{x}=494$g. Test at the 5% level whether the mean is less than 500g, using $z=\dfrac{\bar{x}-\mu_0}{\sigma/\sqrt{n}}$ and critical value $-1.645$.
questions.answer: $z=\dfrac{494-500}{15/\sqrt{36}}=\dfrac{-6}{2.5}=-2.4$. Since $-2.4<-1.645$, we reject $H_0$. There is significant evidence at the 5% level that the mean fill weight is less than $500$g.

questions.q: A population has known standard deviation $\sigma=8$. A sample of $n=64$ has mean $\bar{x}=103$, against a claimed mean $\mu_0=100$. Test at the 1% level whether the mean exceeds 100, using critical value $z^*=2.326$.
questions.answer: $z=\dfrac{103-100}{8/\sqrt{64}}=\dfrac{3}{1}=3$. Since $3>2.326$, we reject $H_0$. There is significant evidence at the 1% level that the mean exceeds $100$.

sections.heading: Two-tailed tests for a population mean

questions.q: A standardized test historically has mean $\mu_0=100$ with $\sigma=15$. A sample of $n=25$ students taking a new prep course has mean $\bar{x}=107$. Test at the 5% level (two-tailed) whether the course changes the mean score, using critical values $\pm1.96$.
questions.answer: $z=\dfrac{107-100}{15/\sqrt{25}}=\dfrac{7}{3}\approx2.333$. Since $|2.333|>1.96$, we reject $H_0$. There is significant evidence at the 5% level that the prep course changes the mean score.

questions.q: Using $z\approx2.33$ from the previous problem, find the two-tailed $p$-value, given $\Phi(2.33)\approx0.9901$, and confirm the conclusion.
questions.answer: $p\text{-value}=2(1-\Phi(2.33))=2(1-0.9901)=2(0.0099)=0.0198$. Since $0.0198<0.05$, we reject $H_0$, confirming the earlier conclusion.

questions.q: A sample of $n=50$ has mean $\bar{x}=48.2$, against a claimed mean $\mu_0=50$ with $\sigma=6$. Test at the 5% level (two-tailed) whether the mean differs from 50, using critical values $\pm1.96$.
questions.answer: $z=\dfrac{48.2-50}{6/\sqrt{50}}=\dfrac{-1.8}{0.8485}\approx-2.121$. Since $|-2.121|>1.96$, we reject $H_0$. There is significant evidence at the 5% level that the mean differs from $50$.

sections.heading: Hypothesis test for a Poisson mean

questions.q: A website historically crashes at a rate of $\lambda_0=4$ per month. After a software update, 1 crash is observed in a randomly selected month. Test at the 5% level whether the crash rate has decreased, using $P(X\leq1)\approx0.0916$ for $X\sim\text{Po}(4)$.
questions.answer: $H_0:\lambda=4$. $H_a:\lambda<4$. $p\text{-value}=P(X\leq1)=0.0916$. Since $0.0916>0.05$, we do not reject $H_0$. There is insufficient evidence at the 5% level that the crash rate has decreased.

questions.q: Explain why an exact Poisson probability, rather than a normal approximation, is used to test a hypothesis about a Poisson mean when $\lambda_0$ is small.
questions.answer: When $\lambda_0$ is small, the Poisson distribution is noticeably skewed and a normal approximation would be unreliable, so exact Poisson probabilities give a more accurate $p$-value.

questions.q: A call center historically receives calls at $\lambda_0=6$ per hour. During a promotional event, 12 calls are received in one hour. Test at the 5% level whether the call rate has increased, using $P(X\geq12)\approx0.0201$ for $X\sim\text{Po}(6)$.
questions.answer: $H_0:\lambda=6$. $H_a:\lambda>6$. $p\text{-value}=P(X\geq12)=0.0201$. Since $0.0201<0.05$, we reject $H_0$. There is significant evidence at the 5% level that the call rate has increased during the promotional event.

questions.q: A factory's defect rate is historically $\lambda_0=3$ per shift. During a trial of new equipment, 8 defects are observed in one shift. Test at the 5% level whether the defect rate has increased, using $P(X\geq8)\approx0.0119$ for $X\sim\text{Po}(3)$.
questions.answer: $H_0:\lambda=3$. $H_a:\lambda>3$. $p\text{-value}=P(X\geq8)=0.0119$. Since $0.0119<0.05$, we reject $H_0$. There is significant evidence at the 5% level that the defect rate has increased.

sections.heading: Hypothesis test for a binomial proportion

questions.q: A company claims $40\%$ of its customers use its mobile app ($p_0=0.4$). In a sample of $n=15$ customers, 10 report using the app. Test at the 5% level whether the true proportion is greater than 40%, using $P(X\geq10)\approx0.0338$ for $X\sim B(15,0.4)$.
questions.answer: $H_0:p=0.4$. $H_a:p>0.4$. $p\text{-value}=P(X\geq10)=0.0338$. Since $0.0338<0.05$, we reject $H_0$. There is significant evidence at the 5% level that more than 40% of customers use the app.

questions.q: Explain why the binomial hypothesis test uses the exact binomial distribution rather than a normal approximation when $n$ is small.
questions.answer: For small $n$, the binomial distribution can be quite skewed (especially if $p_0$ is far from $0.5$), so a normal approximation would be unreliable; exact binomial probabilities give a more accurate $p$-value.

questions.q: A coin is tested for fairness ($p_0=0.5$). In 20 tosses, 6 heads are observed. Test at the 5% level (two-tailed) whether the coin is biased, using $P(X\leq6)\approx0.0577$ for $X\sim B(20,0.5)$ (doubled for a two-tailed test).
questions.answer: $H_0:p=0.5$. $H_a:p\neq0.5$. Two-tailed $p\text{-value}=2\times P(X\leq6)=2(0.0577)=0.1154$. Since $0.1154>0.05$, we do not reject $H_0$. There is insufficient evidence at the 5% level that the coin is biased.

questions.q: A politician claims $60\%$ of voters support a new policy ($p_0=0.6$). In a sample of 12 voters, only 3 support it. Test at the 5% level whether support is less than 60%, using $P(X\leq3)\approx0.0153$ for $X\sim B(12,0.6)$.
questions.answer: $H_0:p=0.6$. $H_a:p<0.6$. $p\text{-value}=P(X\leq3)=0.0153$. Since $0.0153<0.05$, we reject $H_0$. There is significant evidence at the 5% level that support is less than 60%.

sections.heading: Type I and Type II errors, and significance level

questions.q: In the website crash-rate test, describe what a Type I error would mean in context, and what a Type II error would mean.
questions.answer: A Type I error would mean concluding the crash rate has decreased when it actually hasn't (rejecting a true $H_0$) — wrongly crediting the software update. A Type II error would mean failing to detect a real decrease in the crash rate (failing to reject a false $H_0$) — missing genuine improvement from the update.

questions.q: Explain what is meant by the significance level of a hypothesis test, and state the probability of a Type I error in a test conducted at the 5% significance level.
questions.answer: The significance level $\alpha$ is the probability of rejecting a true null hypothesis (a Type I error), chosen in advance by the person conducting the test. At the 5% significance level, $\alpha=0.05$, so there is a 5% probability of a Type I error.

questions.q: A researcher conducts a test at $\alpha=0.10$ instead of the more common $\alpha=0.05$. Explain how this affects the probability of Type I and Type II errors, compared to using $\alpha=0.05$.
questions.answer: Using a larger $\alpha=0.10$ increases the probability of a Type I error (the rejection region is larger, so a true $H_0$ is more likely to be rejected by chance) but decreases the probability of a Type II error (it becomes easier to reject $H_0$, so a false $H_0$ is more likely to be correctly rejected) — there is a direct tradeoff between the two error types as $\alpha$ changes.

sections.heading: A well-designed word problem: testing a new manufacturing process

questions.q: This question has four parts. A factory's current process produces components with mean breaking strength $\mu_0=250$ N and known $\sigma=20$ N. A new process gives a sample of $n=40$ components with mean $\bar{x}=257$ N. (a) State $H_0$ and $H_a$ for testing whether the new process increases mean breaking strength (one-tailed). (b) Compute the test statistic $z$. (c) Using critical value $z^*=1.645$ (5% level), state the conclusion. (d) Quality control also monitors defects; the historical rate is $\lambda_0=5$ per batch, but a batch from the new process has only 1 defect. Using $P(X\leq1)\approx0.0404$ for $X\sim\text{Po}(5)$, test at the 5% level whether the new process has reduced the defect rate.
questions.answer: (a) $H_0:\mu=250$. $H_a:\mu>250$. (b) $z=\dfrac{257-250}{20/\sqrt{40}}=\dfrac{7}{3.1623}\approx2.214$. (c) Since $2.214>1.645$, we reject $H_0$: significant evidence at the 5% level that the new process increases mean breaking strength. (d) $H_0:\lambda=5$, $H_a:\lambda<5$. $p\text{-value}=P(X\leq1)=0.0404<0.05$, so we reject $H_0$: significant evidence at the 5% level that the new process has reduced the defect rate.
